product.title: Dutch 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Dutch: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Dutch builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Dutch is English's close cousin — *huis*, *water*, *boek*, *melk* read themselves — so this course focuses on the spots that actually trip English speakers up, from de versus het to the verb that gets thrown to the end of the sentence. Includes a sound guide (ui, ij, g, eu, oe), an A1 grammar summary, a table of irregular verbs, and lifesaver phrases.

blocks.text: Dutch is often introduced the wrong way: as "English spoken backwards", as a language you don't need because everyone in Amsterdam speaks English anyway. Yet it's a living language for 24 million people, the language of a country where tens of thousands of foreigners study and work, and — this is rarely noticed — **one of English's closest relatives**.

You already know more Dutch than you think. *Huis* (house), *water*, *boek* (book), *melk* (milk), *appel*, *hand*, *bed*, *warm*, *koud* (cold), *zon* (sun). English has even borrowed straight from Dutch: *cookie* (koekje), *boss* (baas), *yacht* (jacht), *skate*, *landscape* (landschap), *brandy* (brandewijn). This course takes advantage of that from Unit 1: you don't start from zero, you start from a few hundred words already in your head.

Only three things are truly new, and none of them has an English equivalent. **First**, every noun takes either *de* or *het* — and there's no rule you can really rely on to guess which. **Second**, the Dutch verb must sit in second place in a statement, so *tomorrow I go* becomes *morgen ga ik* — "tomorrow go I". **Third**, in a subordinate clause the verb is thrown to the very end: *omdat ik moe ben*, "because I tired am".

This course tackles all three early instead of saving them for the last chapter: *de/het* is set up in Unit 3, word order gets a whole unit in Unit 10, and subordinate clauses close the course in Unit 20 — not because they are the hardest, but because that's where everything you've learned finally connects into a story.
The explanations are short on purpose. What's long isn't the theory, it's the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read out loud. The sounds *g*, *ui* and *ij* will never stick if you only read them in your head — you'll memorize the spelling, not the language.

From the very first unit, learn nouns **together with their de or het**: not *huis*, but *het huis*. That one little word decides the form of adjectives, *this/that* and pronouns throughout the sentence later on.

Don't wait until your sounds are perfect before you dare to speak. The Dutch will switch to English the moment they hear an accent — just keep answering in Dutch, and nine times out of ten they'll switch back.

blocks.text: Enjoy the course. *Veel succes!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Dutch out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears do the work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it is where you see how Dutch *thinks*. Example: *Ik heet Budi* literally means "I am-called Budi", and *Hoe gaat het?* means "how goes it?".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation. Nouns are always given with *de* or *het*, so their group sticks too.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Dutch, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Dutch sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. The "Say it" column in every vocabulary table is not decoration — it's a core part of the lesson.

The good news first: Dutch spelling is **honest**. Once you know the sound of each letter and letter combination, you can read words you've never seen and almost always get them right — something impossible in English or Danish. All you need to learn is the list, and the list is short.

The **Say it** column throughout this course is written to be read the way an English speaker naturally would, with capital letters marking the stressed syllable. Example: *bedankt* → **buh-DANGKT**, stress on the second syllable. **uh** is the weak vowel in "*a*bout"; **ay** as in "day" (but without the glide); **ee** as in "see"; **oo** as in "moon"; **e** as in "bed"; **i** as in "bit"; **a** is short, as in British "hot" or a clipped "father", while **ah** is the long "father" sound; **o** as in British "lot", **oh** as in "go" but without the glide. Dutch stress usually falls on the first syllable, except in loanwords and words starting with *be-*, *ge-*, *ver-*, *ont-*.
Long and short vowels — a difference that changes meaning
English has long and short vowels too, but they differ in quality ("bit" vs "beat"). In Dutch the same vowel is simply held longer — and the length alone tells words apart.

The rule: **double** vowels (aa, ee, oo, uu) are always long. A **single** vowel is long when it ends an open syllable — that's why *maken* is read MAH-kuh(n) even though it's written with one *a*, while *makkelijk* with two *k*'s makes the vowel short. **ü** (Dutch *u/uu*) has no English match: say "ee" with your lips rounded as if for "oo" — the French *u* or German *ü*.

blocks.text: *ij* and *ei* are pronounced **exactly the same**; the only difference is spelling, and the Dutch themselves call them *lange ij* and *korte ei* to tell them apart when spelling. No rule decides which is used — you learn it word by word.
The most feared sounds: ui, g and sch

**ui.** This sound doesn't exist in any language you're likely to know, and it's the only Dutch sound that really needs practice. How to do it: shape your mouth for "ö" (as in *deur*), then, without moving your lips, slide your tongue towards "ee". The result is a gliding sound written **öy** in this course. The closest English gets is "ow" in "how" said with rounded lips.

**g and ch.** Both are pronounced the same: a rough, scraping sound at the back of the throat, like *ch* in Scottish **loch** or German **Bach**, but harsher and hissier. In this course it's written **kh**. Never the *g* of "go". In the south (Brabant, Limburg and all of Belgium) the sound is much softer — both are equally correct.

**sch** = s + kh, two sounds in a row, never "sh" or "sk": *school* → **skhohl**, *schrijven* → **SKHREY-fuh(n)**. But at the **end** of a word, *-isch* is said **-is**: *logisch* → LOH-khis, *Indonesisch* → in-do-NAY-zis.

blocks.title: Sound habits that change everything
items: **Word endings harden.** A final *d* is said **t** and a final *b* is said **p**: *hond* → hont (dog), *ik heb* → ik hep, *hij wordt* → hey vort. The spelling stays; only the sound changes.

**The -en ending loses its n.** *lopen* → LOH-puh, *wonen* → VOH-nuh, *de mensen* → duh MEN-suh. In everyday speech the final *n* is almost always dropped; this course writes it as **(n)** to remind you it's there on paper but not in the mouth.
**Unstressed e = uh**, like the "a" in "about": *de* (duh), *een* (uhn) = a, *gesproken* (khuh-SPROH-kuh).
⚠️ Stressed *een* means **one** and is said **ayn**; unstressed it's the article "a" and is said **uhn**. When it needs to be clear, the Dutch write it *één*.

blocks.text: Practice these five words until they're smooth before starting Unit 1 — between them they hold all the typical Dutch sounds: *goedemorgen* (KHOO-duh-mor-khuh), *alstublieft* (as-tü-BLEEFT), *uitstekend* (ÖYT-stay-kuhnt), *misschien* (mi-SKHEEN), *dank je wel* (dangk yuh VEL).

All the grammar of this course in ten tables. This section is meant to be opened again months after the last unit — when you can already speak, but have forgotten why something is written the way it is.
1. Articles & plurals
Plural: **-en** for almost every word; **-s** after -el, -em, -en, -er, -je and after an unstressed vowel (*auto's*). All plurals take *de*.
2. Pronouns
3. Present-tense verbs
When *jij/je* comes **after** the verb, the *-t* disappears: *woon je?*, *ga je?* — but not with *u*: *woont u?*
4. Helper verbs
⚠️ *Je moet niet* = **you mustn't**. "You don't have to" = *je hoeft niet te …*
5. Word order
The rest of the sentence follows the order **time → manner → place**: *Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Utrecht.*

blocks.text: Thirty-six verbs, ordered by how often you'll need them. The second column is the simple past (used for states and stories), the third is the past participle (used with *hebben*/*zijn*). A **z** means the verb takes *zijn*.
Don't learn them all at once. Mark the ten you use most, stick them on the wall, and swap the list every two weeks.
Twenty sentences that cover almost every conversational emergency. If you forget everything else in this course, these are what should remain.

blocks.title: Five little words that make you sound native
items: **even** — softens a request: *Kun je me even helpen?*
**hoor** — softens a statement: *Nee hoor.*
**wel** — the opposite of *niet*, for emphasis: *Ik wel!*
**maar** — softens a command: *Ga maar zitten.*
**gezellig** — the highest praise for any atmosphere: cozy, sociable, fun all at once.
